```{r}
#| label: ca-income-setup
#| include: false 
library(ggplot2)
source('income.R')
```

```{r}
#| label: load-ca-data
#| cache: true
california.state.code = 6
ca_income = income(california.state.code)
```

```{r}
#| label: make-ca-maps
# Make maps of California with and without population density shown

ca.plot = ggplot(data=ca_income$info, mapping=aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group)) + 
  coord_quickmap() +
  geom_polygon(fill='gray', color = "white", alpha=.4) +
      scale_fill_gradient(trans="log10") + 
      theme_void()

ca.pop.plot = ggplot(data=ca_income$info, mapping=aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group)) + 
  coord_quickmap() +
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = pop/area), color = "white") +
      scale_fill_gradient(trans="log10") + 
      theme_void()
```


```{r}
#| label: fake-ca-population
#| cache: true

# For illustration purposes, we're going to make up a fake population that we can think of our sample as being drawn from. 
# We'll make up a population as follows
# 1. choose the number of people to be the number of people in our sample scaled up to account for the cps sampling ratio. 
#    Or, really, a smaller ratio that's more usable visually.
# 2. draw units with replacement from the sample to get a set of rows to *add to the sample* to get the population
# 3. tweak these new rows to make them a bit different 
#  - perturb the income in these new rows by income by multiplying by 1*.1U for U uniform on [-1, 1]. 
#  - perturb their location by resampling their location from their subregion
# 4. combine the sample and the added rows to get the population, shuffling so the sample isn't at the top
#    we'll save the indices of the sample rows in the population as 'J' so we can refer to them later.

earnings = ca_income$sample
earnings$degree = factor(earnings$education >= 16, # we use this dichotomization a lot early on
                         levels=c(FALSE, TRUE),
                         labels=c('no 4-year degree','4-year degree')) 
earnings$group = 1                     # we need this for mapping
cps.sampling.ratio = 1/2500            # the actual one
plotting.cps.sampling.ratio=1/12.5     # works visually
npop = nrow(earnings) / plotting.cps.sampling.ratio
pop.seed = 1

newtopop = earnings[(\()sample(1:nrow(earnings), npop-nrow(earnings), replace=TRUE)) |> with_seed(pop.seed), ]
newtopop$income = newtopop$income*(1 + .1 * runif(nrow(newtopop), -1, 1))
newlocations = ca_income$sample_location(newtopop$county, seed=2)
newtopop$lat  = newlocations$lat
newtopop$long = newlocations$long
pop.earnings = rbind(earnings, newtopop)

order = (\() sample(1:nrow(pop.earnings))) |> with_seed(pop.seed)
J=order[1:nrow(earnings)]
pop.earnings[order, ] = pop.earnings
```


```{r}
#| label:  define-old-names-for-ca-stuff

# Now we'll define a bunch of stuff that's used in older lectures
# where the fake population and sample had a more awkward relationship

display.population = pop.earnings
pop.tab = pop.earnings

our.sample = earnings 
sample.tab = earnings
sample.tab$J = J
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-ca-sample-and-population

# Now we'll plot the sample and the population on the map.
# Probably in the future this should be done in the lecture file,
# as we may want them colored differently lecture by lecture.
sample.plot = ca.plot + geom_point(aes(x=long, y=lat), data=earnings, size=.2, alpha=.5)
sample.plot.inf = ca.pop.plot + geom_point(aes(x=long, y=lat), data=earnings, size=.2, alpha=.5)
pop.plot = ca.plot + geom_point(aes(x=long, y=lat), data=pop.earnings, size=.02, alpha=.1) 
pop.plot.inf = ca.pop.plot + geom_point(aes(x=long, y=lat), data=pop.earnings, size=.01, alpha=.1)  
```

```{r}
#| label: visualization-defaults

## default settings for our scatter plot
scale_y = function(limits=c(0, 2e5)) { 
  list(scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0, max(limits), by=25e3), labels=label_dollar()),
       coord_cartesian(ylim=limits))
}
years = 8:20
scale_x = function(limits=c(min(years)-.5, max(years)+.5)) { 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=years, labels=sprintf('%dy', years), limits=limits)
}
dot.size = 2
```
